explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Matthew says, "His face shone like the sun…" Peter, James and John saw it right in front of them. I'd have needed oven mitts for my eyeballs.

explanations.answer: It turns as pale as ash
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. The text says, "His face shone like the sun…" It describes a shine, and pale ash isn't in the picture. Ash is what I get when I forget the timer on a batch, and nothing about this scene looks like that.
No veil in this story, baker. Matthew says, "There He was transfigured before them." Before them means out in the open, right in front of Peter, James and John. No curtain, no "come back later."

You got it. "Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus." Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36). Two giants from Israel's long past, and they just show up on a mountaintop. I'd need a minute to sit down.

Great names, baker, but they're not the ones on this mountain. Abraham was the father of Isaac (Genesis 21:3), and both are from Israel's long past. Matthew says it was "…Moses and Elijah…" who appeared with Jesus. Pretty good guess for a mountain full of surprises.

Nice try, friend. David was Israel's king, and Solomon sat on the throne of his father David (1 Kings 2:12). But they aren't the two on this mountain. Matthew says, "Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them…"

Not quite, baker. They don't stand there silent. Matthew says Moses and Elijah appeared "…talking with Jesus." It was a real conversation. I'd love to know what was said, but the text doesn't tell us.

That's right. Moses and Elijah are not silent statues. The text says they appeared "…talking with Jesus." Picture a quiet mountaintop where three people are having a conversation, and Peter, James and John get to watch.

That's the one. Peter says, "…I will put up three shelters…" One for Jesus, one for Moses and one for Elijah. The man is offering to do construction in the middle of a miracle, and I respect the energy.

Altars sound very holy, friend, and I'd have guessed them too. But Peter never says that word. He says, "…I will put up three shelters…" Shelters are what he offers, and the text keeps it that simple.
Pillars aren't part of Peter's offer, baker. He says, "…I will put up three shelters…" Same plan, one for each of the three, but the word is shelters. Stone never gets mentioned.

You got it, baker. The voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!" It speaks about Jesus and calls Him Son. It's the clearest introduction on the whole mountain.

Not this one, friend. The voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!" Prophet isn't the word used. Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36) and he was right there on the mountain, but the voice speaks about Jesus as Son.

Good try, baker, but that's not the title. The voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Servant is a fair guess, but the voice picks a different word, and it's a family word: Son. Then it adds that it is well pleased with Him.
Yes, baker. The voice says, "Listen to Him!" Peter was still speaking when the cloud wrapped around them. I talk a LOT, so I take that line personally. Good news is, it's a fine thing to practice.
Fair guess, since Peter had just been speaking. But the voice says, "Listen to Him!" The word is listen. And friend, I'm the one who can't stop talking, so that one lands on me too.
Reasonable guess, baker, but the text doesn't say pray. The voice says, "Listen to Him!" It comes after the voice says it is well pleased with Jesus. The command is short and clear.

That's right, baker. Matthew says, "When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror." They had just heard a voice from the cloud. I dive face first into chocolate chips for fun, but they hit the ground out of terror.

Not this time, friend. Matthew says, "When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror." That's Peter, James and John, right after the voice from the cloud. It was real terror, and they went straight to the ground.
You got it. Jesus says, "Get up… Do not be afraid." He touched them first, and then He spoke. The three of them had just fallen facedown in terror, so I think that touch meant a lot.

Close to something He says later, baker, but not here. On the mountain Jesus tells them, "Get up… Do not be afraid." Later, on the way down, He tells them not to tell anyone about the vision. Different moment, different words.
Good try, friend, but shame isn't in this verse. Jesus touches them and says, "Get up… Do not be afraid." They had fallen facedown in terror, and His words answer that fear. Nothing else gets added.

Not quite, baker. Matthew says that when they looked up, "…they saw no one except Jesus." Moses and Elijah weren't among the ones they saw. When the three disciples looked up, the only one they saw was Jesus.
That's right. The text says, "…they saw no one except Jesus." Moses and Elijah were gone from view. After all that glow, cloud and voice, it ends with Jesus, right there with them.

explanations.answer: Until He is raised from the dead
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead." That's the timeline He gives them. I can't hold a secret for five minutes, so I'm impressed.

explanations.answer: Until they reach the city of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend, but no city comes up in this command. Jesus says, "Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead." The condition is His being raised. The text doesn't mention a place to reach first.

explanations.answer: Until the Passover feast has ended
explanations.explanation: Close to a calendar answer, baker, but the text doesn't name any feast. Jesus says, "Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead." That's the timeline in this passage.

Not this time, baker. Jesus doesn't say the scribes are mixed up. He says, "Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things." So Elijah does come, and Jesus goes on to say he has already come.
You got it. Jesus says, "Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things." He doesn't say the scribes have it mixed up. Then He adds that Elijah has already come.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands." I think this one is heavy, so I'll keep it simple. Back in verse 9 He also mentions being raised from the dead, so both are part of what He says.

Not the word in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands." It's a heavy thing to hear. The word He uses is suffer, and He says it in the same way as what was done to Elijah.

That's not the word here, baker. Jesus says, "In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands." It's a heavy line, and it's about what people will do to Him. He also talks about being raised from the dead in verse 9.

That's right, baker. The text says, "Then the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist." John the Baptist came preaching in the Desert of Judea (Matthew 3:1). The lightbulb goes off right there on the mountain path.

Good name, baker, but not the one Jesus means. Isaiah was a prophet (Matthew 3:3), but the text says the disciples understood "…He was speaking to them about John the Baptist." That's who Jesus was talking about.

That's a smart guess, friend. Elisha followed Elijah and became his servant (1 Kings 19:21). But Matthew says the disciples understood "…He was speaking to them about John the Baptist." That's the name the text gives.
